reading.rtitle: The Number Nobody Read Out Loud
paras: The slide said 3.4, and for eleven months nobody in the room asked what it was 3.4 of. It sat in the same corner of the same monthly pack, under a heading that had been copied forward so many times that the heading no longer described the figure underneath it. It was, in fact, a ratio: two numbers divided by each other. Both of them had changed. The result had not.

It was Priya Menon who asked, in her second month. She had come from a manufacturing company and she did not know what anything in the pack meant yet, which is why she asked the question that people who understood the pack had stopped asking. Not is it good. She asked somebody to read the line out loud, in words, from left to right. Nobody could. Three people tried, and each of them said something different.

What came out over the following week was not an error. Everything netted off correctly and the margin was where it should be. What was wrong was smaller and more expensive than an error. The ratio had been rounded to one decimal place in 2019, when the numbers were much smaller, and at the current size that rounding hid a movement of almost four hundred thousand every month. The team had been comparing themselves against a benchmark that had been calculated on a different basis. And the line that was supposed to show whether the region would break even could not answer that question at all, because the costs it excluded had grown from immaterial to a fifth of the total.

Priya now opens every review the same way, and it takes ninety seconds. Somebody reads one line of the pack out loud, in full sentences, and says what it is a proportion of. “Half the mistakes I have ever found,” she says, “were found by somebody saying a number out loud and hearing that it did not make sense. Not by anybody checking it. By somebody saying it.”

listenings.text: A small thing that costs people credibility, and almost nobody is taught it. If a rate goes from four per cent to six per cent, that is not a two per cent increase. It is an increase of two percentage points, and it is also a fifty per cent increase. Those are three different numbers describing exactly the same movement, and if you pick the wrong one the person listening will either think it is tiny or think it is enormous. I have watched a room approve something because somebody said two per cent, when the honest sentence was that the rate went up by half. So here is the rule I use. Say the two numbers first, from and to. Four to six. Then say the movement, and say which kind it is. Nobody has ever been criticised for being that clear, and it takes one extra second.

When I present numbers to people who do not work with them all day, I use three sentences per figure and never more. The first sentence is the number and what it is a proportion of. Not just three point four. Three point four times our monthly fixed costs. The second sentence is the comparison, and I always give the direction and the size together: that is up from two point nine last year, so roughly twenty per cent higher. The third sentence is what it means, in words that have nothing to do with accounting: at this level we cover our costs by the middle of the month. Three sentences. And if I cannot say the third one, I have learned that it is because I do not understand the figure yet, and no slide is going to fix that for me.
